description:
We are QuadCore, a team of four innovators passionate about space exploration, AI, and technology. Our expertise includes Full-Stack Development, Python & Machine Learning, Physics Research, and Graphic Design. By combining science, creativity, and technology, we aim to solve real-world challenges through innovative solutions at the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

Four Minds. One Mission. Infinite Possibilities. 🚀
summary:
LUNA-01 is a browser game for children ages 7–12. Players choose an astronaut, read a short mission briefing, and explore a 3D Moon outpost. At the Solar Array, they clean the panels and decide how much power to send to the oxygen generator. At the Greenhouse, they water a seedling, turn on the grow lights, harvest the crop, and store it for the crew. At the Storm Shelter, they power the shielding and radio Earth once the crew is safe.

A Python simulator updates the game’s readings so players can see the consequences of their choices. For example, keeping the grow lights on can leave too little power for the oxygen generator, causing the crew’s oxygen reserve to drop. Players can retry a mission, see how a different choice changes the result, and earn badges that unlock Horizon Base. Our goal is to help young learners understand why astronauts must balance limited resources and give teachers and parents a way to discuss those decisions with children.

We built the game with React, TypeScript, Three.js, and Python, using GitHub for source control and Vercel for hosting. To make it easier to try, we added keyboard and touch controls, short instructions, and an illustrated map for devices without WebGL. The game needs no account or special equipment. The storm scenario draws on an event observed by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, and the simulated radio reply uses NASA’s estimate for direct Earth–Moon signal travel time.
details:
LUNA-01 is an educational browser game where children ages 7–12 take charge of a Moon outpost. Players choose an astronaut, follow a short briefing, and walk to three mission stations. At the Solar Array, they clean the panels and decide how much power to send to the oxygen generator. In the Greenhouse, they water a seedling, turn on the grow lights, harvest the crop, and store food for the crew. At the Storm Shelter, they power the shielding, protect the crew, and radio Earth when the storm passes.

A Python simulator calculates how each decision affects the base. For example, keeping the grow lights on can leave less power for the oxygen generator, causing the crew’s oxygen reserve to fall. Players can see the readings change, retry a mission, and compare the results of different choices. Each completed mission earns a badge, and all three badges unlock Horizon Base. The game connects decisions to places children can explore and tasks they can carry out.

Our goal is to help young learners understand why astronauts must balance limited resources. Teachers and parents can use the missions to start a discussion about what a player chose, what happened, and what they would try next. The storm scenario draws on a real event observed by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. The radio reply delay is based on NASA’s estimate of direct Earth–Moon signal travel time. Resource values and radiation thresholds are simplified for play.

We built the interface with React and TypeScript, the 3D outpost with Three.js, and the simulation API with Python. We used GitHub for version control and Vercel for hosting. We considered energy trade-offs, accessibility, and cost. The game supports keyboard and touch controls, provides an illustrated map for devices without WebGL, and requires no account, installation, or specialized hardware. The Greenhouse shows one action at a time to make it easier for younger players to follow.
